taxonomy_heading.text: OmniTaskonomy: A Unified Taxonomy of Visual Capabilities

source.raw_tex: \section{\methodname: A Unified Taxonomy of Visual Capabilities}

taxonomy_lead.text: We introduce OmniTaskonomy, a shared hierarchy that relates I2I tasks to understanding capabilities based on the visual information they require, rather than their output modality.

source.raw_tex: We introduce \methodname, a shared hierarchy that relates I2I tasks to understanding capabilities based on the visual information they require, rather than their output modality.

taxonomy_caption.text: A unified taxonomy of visual tasks organized into three broad families: Recognition, Reconstruction, and Reorganization. Each leaf is explicitly typed as either an I2I task or an understanding capability, allowing the two modalities to share the same visual hierarchy without conflating their task identities.

source.raw_tex: A unified taxonomy of visual tasks organized into three broad families: \textit{Recognition}, \textit{Reconstruction}, and \textit{Reorganization}. Each leaf is explicitly typed as either an I2I task or an understanding capability, allowing the two modalities to share the same visual hierarchy without conflating their task identities.

taxonomy_annotation.text: Once the capability is finalized, we assign each I2T benchmark sample to a capability leaf. To scale this annotation, we use three independent LLM judges to label each sample using the finalized taxonomy definitions and annotation guidelines. We keep a sample when at least two of the three judges agree on the same capability and use the majority label as its final assignment, and samples without a two-of-three consensus are excluded.

related_example.text: Counting improves with all 19 sources, with 14 gains reaching p<0.05. Localization and object pointing yield the largest observed gains (+3.70 and +3.57 pp, respectively; both p<0.001): both objectives require identifying and locating objects.

source.raw_tex: Counting improves with all 19 sources, with 14 gains reaching $p<0.05$. Localization and object pointing yield the largest observed gains ($+3.70$ and $+3.57$ pp, respectively; both $p<0.001$): both objectives require identifying and locating objects.

depth_example.text: Geometry supervision also benefits metric 3D relation: Z-depth, Euclidean depth, and surface normals improve accuracy by 2.90, 2.77, and 2.49 pp, respectively (all p<0.03).

source.raw_tex: Geometry supervision also benefits metric 3D relation: Z-depth, Euclidean depth, and surface normals improve accuracy by $2.90$, $2.77$, and $2.49$ pp, respectively (all $p<0.03$).
\paragraph{Different sources benefit complementary capabilities.}

cross_results.text: Attribute editing improves category recognition (+2.81 pp, p<0.01), and object editing improves 2D ordering (+8.42 pp, p<0.03). Inpainting and 2.5D segmentation also improve ordering (+9.47 and +11.58 pp), while colorization gives the largest observed gain on visual correspondence (+5.71 pp; all three p<0.01).

source.raw_tex: Attribute editing improves category recognition ($+2.81$ pp, $p<0.01$), and object editing improves 2D ordering ($+8.42$ pp, $p<0.03$). Inpainting and 2.5D segmentation also improve ordering ($+9.47$ and $+11.58$ pp), while colorization gives the largest observed gain on visual correspondence ($+5.71$ pp; all three $p<0.01$).
